title: Design a Vending Machine
tagline: Model a machine whose buttons mean different things in different states, and handle jams, missing change and power loss.

statement.prompt: Design the software for a **vending machine** that sells snacks and drinks. Customers insert money, choose a product and receive the item and change.
context: This is an **object-oriented design** interview. The focus is classes, state, patterns and edge cases.
You can assume the hardware (coin slot, motor, display) exposes simple methods.
Think about what happens when something goes wrong halfway.
given: The machine has up to **40 slots**, each holding one product with a price and quantity.
It accepts **coins and notes** and returns change.
It must keep working with **no network**.
An admin restocks and collects cash.

expectations.title: Drive the conversation
expectations.body: Ask questions before drawing anything. State your assumptions out loud so they can be corrected early.

expectations.title: Use numbers
expectations.body: Turn the givens into requests per second, storage and bandwidth. Every later choice should point back to one of them.

expectations.title: Start simple, then evolve
expectations.body: Get a working version on the board first. Add caches, sharding and queues only when a number or a requirement asks for them.

expectations.title: Go deep on the hard parts
expectations.body: For this problem the hard parts are modelling behaviour by state, making change correctly, and failure cases like jams and power loss.

expectations.title: Name the trade-offs
expectations.body: Say what you chose, what you gave up, and what would make you change your mind.

expectations.title: Think about failure
expectations.body: Point out single points of failure and say what happens when a node, a cache or a whole zone goes down.

great: Uses the **State pattern** and can list the states and events.
Handles jams, sold-out items and power loss.

concepts.def: An object changes its behaviour when its internal state changes; each state is a class.
A move from one state to another caused by an event, such as Idle to HasMoney when a coin is inserted.
Return the largest coin that fits, repeatedly. Works for common currencies.
Two writers read the same value and one overwrites the other's change.
The device works fully without a connection and syncs later.

numbers: Change = money paid - price. Use the **largest coin first**
Persist **balance and state** so a power cut cannot lose the customer's money

takeaways: Model behaviour with the **State pattern**: Idle, HasMoney, Dispensing, OutOfService.
**Validate first, act last**: stock and change are checked before the motor runs.
Plan for jams, no change, power loss and concurrent admin/user access.
Use **Strategy** for payment methods so UPI or cards can be added later.

steps.title: What should it do?
steps.prompt: Which features are in the **core** scope for a snack vending machine?
steps.hint: Walk a customer through from walking up to walking away.
steps.explain: Core: **insert money, select, dispense, change, cancel/refund, restock.** Ask which coins and notes are accepted.

notes: Core: insert money, select product, dispense, return change, cancel/refund, admin restock

options.text: Cancel and refund the inserted money
options.why: Every real machine has this.

options.text: Dispense the product and return the correct change
options.why: Money out.

options.text: Accept coins and notes and track the balance
options.why: Money in.

options.text: Admin can restock and collect cash
options.why: Keeps the machine useful.

options.text: Cloud analytics and dynamic pricing
options.why: A backend add-on. Mention it as an extension.

options.text: Let the user select a product by code
options.why: Choice.

steps.title: Find the classes
steps.prompt: Which of these deserve to be classes?
steps.hint: What changes how a button behaves?
steps.explain: Look for **things that have behaviour or rules**. The surprise is that **states are classes** too.

notes: Classes: VendingMachine, Inventory/Slot/Product, Coin/Note, ChangeCalculator, State classes

options.text: State classes (Idle, HasMoney, Dispensing, ...)
options.why: Behaviour depends on state: model each state explicitly.

options.text: VendingMachine
options.why: The coordinator that holds the current state and balance.

options.text: A `Customer` class with a name and age
options.why: The machine does not know customers.

options.text: Coin / Note (money)
options.why: Denominations and value.

options.text: ChangeCalculator
options.why: Separates the maths of making change.

options.text: Inventory and Slot/Product
options.why: Which product is in which slot, with price and quantity.

steps.title: Model the behaviour
steps.prompt: Pressing **Select** does different things when there is no money, enough money, or not enough money. Best way to model this?
steps.hint: Think of a traffic light or a turnstile.
steps.explain: **State pattern.** The machine holds a `state` object and delegates actions to it. A new state (say `Maintenance`) is a new class.

notes: Behaviour: State pattern with Idle, HasMoney, Dispensing, OutOfService

steps.pitfall: Boolean flags instead of explicit states.
steps.followup: How would you draw this as a state-transition table?

options.text: Let the hardware decide
options.why: The logic must live in software you can test.

options.text: Booleans like `hasMoney`, `isDispensing`, `isOutOfStock` checked in every method
options.why: Boolean combinations explode and invalid combinations are possible.

options.text: The **State pattern**: each state is a class with the same methods (`insert_coin`, `select`, `cancel`)
options.why: No giant if/else. Each state decides what each action means.

options.text: One huge `handle(event)` method with nested conditions
options.why: Impossible to extend or test.

steps.title: A purchase, in order
steps.prompt: A user buys a 40-rupee snack with a 50-rupee note. Order the events.
steps.explain: **Validate first, act last.** The irreversible hardware actions come after every check has passed.

notes: Purchase: insert -> select -> validate stock and balance -> dispense -> return change -> Idle

items.text: The user inserts the note; the machine moves from Idle to HasMoney with balance 50
items.why: State changes on the first coin.

items.text: The machine checks stock and that balance >= price
The motor dispenses the item; stock decreases by one
items.why: The irreversible step comes after all checks.

items.text: Change of 10 is returned, balance resets, state returns to Idle
items.why: Machine is ready for the next customer.

steps.title: Making change
steps.prompt: A user paid **100** for an item costing **63**. Coins available: 20, 10, 5, 2, 1. Using the **fewest coins**, how many coins are returned?
steps.hint: Subtract, then take the largest coin that fits each time.
steps.explain: Greedy (largest first) is optimal for normal currency systems. Mention the catch: **the machine may not have those coins**, so check you can make change **before** dispensing.

notes: Change: greedy largest-coin-first; verify change is possible before dispensing

work: Coins returned: 20 + 10 + 5 + 2 = 37, so **4 coins** (the greedy method: largest coin first)

steps.title: What can go wrong?
steps.prompt: Which failure and edge cases should the design handle?
steps.explain: A **state/event table** shows you have covered every combination. Each unexpected cell should map to a safe response.

notes: Edge cases: sold out, no change, jam, power loss, invalid action per state

options.text: Invalid actions in a state (select with no money): ignore with a message
options.why: Define behaviour for every state/action pair.

options.text: Cannot make exact change: tell the user and offer a refund
options.why: Check before dispensing.

options.text: Item jams in the slot: refund and flag the slot
options.why: The motor can fail; plan for it.

options.text: Product sold out: reject the selection and keep the money available
options.why: Do not take money for nothing.

options.text: Power loss mid-vend: save state and balance to durable memory, refund on reboot
options.why: Persist what matters.

options.text: Nothing, a vending machine is simple
options.why: That is the trap in this question.

steps.title: Keeping stock accurate
steps.prompt: Two events: the user buys the last Cola, and an admin restocks Cola at the same time. How do you keep quantity correct?
steps.explain: Even a small machine has two actors. **Serialise access** to inventory.

notes: Inventory: atomic quantity updates (admin and user can overlap)

options.text: Let admin and user share one global flag
options.why: Does not protect the count.

options.text: Make updates to a slot's quantity atomic (a lock, or a single-threaded controller loop)
options.why: Never lose an update.

options.text: Read the quantity, subtract 1 in the UI, write it back
options.why: A classic lost-update race.

options.text: Ignore it: the machine only has one user
options.why: Admin and user can overlap, and software bugs also create overlaps.

steps.title: Which other patterns fit?
steps.prompt: Adding new payment methods (card, UPI QR) later should not rewrite the machine. What helps?
steps.explain: **State** for behaviour, **Strategy** for payment, **Singleton** only if there is exactly one machine object in the process. Name patterns *and* the problem they solve.

notes: Extensibility: PaymentMethod strategy for coins, cards, UPI

options.text: Replace the state machine with one big switch
options.why: Loses the clean structure.

options.text: An if/else on payment type inside `select()`
options.why: Every new method edits core logic.

options.text: Copy the machine class for each payment method
options.why: Duplicate code.

options.text: A `PaymentMethod` interface (Strategy) with Coin, Card and UPI implementations
options.why: Open/closed: add a new class.

steps.title: A fleet of machines
steps.prompt: The company now runs 10,000 machines. What do you add?
steps.hint: What if the network is down?
steps.explain: **Edge-first design**: the machine is authoritative locally and syncs asynchronously. The backend is for visibility and planning.

notes: Fleet: machines work offline; async events to a backend for stock alerts and reports

options.text: Remove local state so machines depend on the server
options.why: Machines must keep working offline.

options.text: Nothing: machines are independent
options.why: The business needs restock routes and reports.

options.text: A central server that must approve every single sale in real time
options.why: A network blip would stop all sales.

options.text: A backend that receives sales, stock and fault events from each machine over a queue, and shows low-stock alerts
options.why: Machines work offline; events flow when connected.

steps.title: Defend your design
steps.prompt: In two or three sentences: why use the State pattern here and what does it cost?
steps.explain: Say **when you would not** use the pattern too. It shows judgement.

notes: Trade-offs: State pattern clarity vs more classes; offline-first vs central control

steps.model: The **State pattern** makes behaviour explicit: each state decides what each action means, which removes boolean flags and makes new states easy. The cost is **more classes** and small amounts of boilerplate. For a machine with only two states a simple switch would be fine; with four or more states and growth expected, the pattern pays off. I also validate everything before the irreversible dispense and persist state against power loss.
points: Explicit states instead of boolean flags
